title: the prayer a room says without a page
hookLine: "Our Father": the family word, plain asks, and two endings
tomorrow: who your neighbor turns out to be
last: JESUS — THE WRONG PEOPLE, ON PURPOSE.

cards: Weddings, funerals, a locker room before a big game. Our Father, who art in heaven. A whole room can say it without anyone holding a page.
Then, near the end, a small awkward moment. Some people stop at deliver us from evil. Others keep going: for thine is the kingdom.
Nobody got it wrong. Here's why, and what the very first word is doing.

teach.b: It opens, in the old English: "Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name." Start with Father. Jesus spoke Aramaic, and once, praying the night before he died, a Gospel keeps his own word: Abba.
The family word, what a child says at home and a grown son still says to his dad. You may have heard it means daddy; scholars push back, since adults used it too.
But it isn't a courtroom title. Then our. Not my.
The whole prayer never once says I, me or my. Even said alone in a quiet room, it assumes a family around you.

Then come the asks: that God's name be honored, that his kingdom come on earth as in heaven, bread for today, forgiveness as we forgive, and rescue from evil. One of those lines changes from church to church.
Some say forgive us our debts, the older wording of the Gospel. Others say trespasses, from an old English prayer book.
And the ending. The oldest copies of the Gospel stop at deliver us from evil. An early Christian handbook has a line of praise after it, and later copies carry the longer ending.
So Catholics usually stop at evil, and at Mass the praise comes a moment later. Protestants usually say it straight through to the amen.

how: Christians pray the Lord's Prayer at home and in church, where the congregation often says it together, aloud. Some churches say "debts" and others "trespasses"; Catholics usually stop at "deliver us from evil" when praying it alone, while Protestant churches usually say it through "for thine is the kingdom" to the amen.

games.q: what's inside the prayer — tap the pairs.

s: the Lord's Prayer never says I, me or my
our, us, our, us: the whole prayer is plural.
the oldest copies end with for thine is the kingdom
they stop at deliver us from evil; later copies carry the longer ending.
abba is baby talk for daddy
it's the family word, but grown children used it too. close, not childish.

games.q: the room is saying the Lord's Prayer. your neighbor stops at deliver us from evil; you keep going. what happened?
o: two churches, two endings, both old.
one of you said a different prayer.
games.why: the oldest copies end at evil; a line of praise was used in prayer very early and appears in later copies. Catholics say it at Mass a moment later.

practice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let your breathing settle. Think of the word our, and let one person you love come to mind.
Then widen it to the people you'll pass today, strangers included. If you pray, you can say the opening line slowly: Our Father, which art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.
If you don't, rest in the word our, and everyone it takes in.

wordCard.voice: The Lord's Prayer. The family word, Abba, Father, then a few plain asks. Eleventh word.

orig.note: Aramaic: father, the family word. one Gospel keeps it untranslated: "Abba, Father."

carryVoice: Your line: you're not addressing a stranger. That's what the first word says. Day eleven, done.
